title: LLM Value Functions for Credit Assignment in Agentic RL

paper.title: LLM Value Functions for Credit Assignment in Agentic RL
paper.abstract:
Abstract Reinforcement learning (RL) for large language model (LLM) agents remains challenging in long-horizon tasks with sparse outcome rewards, where assigning credit to individual actions is difficult.
Methods such as GRPO assign the same trajectory-level advantage to all actions, while critic-based methods require learning an additional value function that can be costly and unstable.
We introduce LLM Value Function RL (LVRL), which uses the pretrained knowledge and in-context learning ability of an LLM to estimate policy-aware state values without finetuning a separate critic.
LVRL conditions the value model on group context and calibrates its predictions using known values at the initial and terminal states, enabling step-level credit assignment from estimated value differences.
We further extend this idea to learning from an expert policy through on-policy distillation (OPD), introducing LLM Value Function OPD (LVOPD), which focuses teacher supervision on actions associated with decreases in estimated value.
We evaluate our approach across diverse agentic benchmarks: AppWorld, BabyAI, and SWE-bench Verified.
Across policy scales (4B to 32B), LVRL consistently and substantially outperforms both GRPO and PPO.
On AppWorld and SWE-bench Verified, LVRL yields absolute improvements of up to 13.6 13.6 and 8.6 8.6 percentage points over GRPO.
Notably, on tasks requiring extended exploration like BabyAI, LVRL raises success from near 0 % 0\% to 75.0 % 75.0\% .
Furthermore, LVOPD yields consistent improvements over standard distillation baselines on AppWorld.
Finally, a Monte-Carlo analysis shows that the frozen critic identifies most semantic pitfalls and recoveries, indicating that LVRL extracts meaningful, policy-aware step-level credit from sparse terminal outcomes.

Reinforcement learning allows these agents to improve from experience, but environment rewards are typically sparse and outcome-based in the form of a single binary signal at the end of the episode indicating success or failure. How to distribute this single bit of feedback across individual actions is the classical problem of temporal credit assignment ( Sutton & Barto, 1998 ) . Current policy optimization methods face a trade-off between coarse trajectory-level credit and the high cost of learning a value function. Outcome-only methods like GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) estimate a group-relative baseline and assign the same scalar advantage to every action in a trajectory. This uniform signal fails to distinguish individual contributions as mistakes in successful trajectories receive positive credit, while useful actions in failed trajectories receive negative credit. Alternatively, methods like PPO ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) learn a value function to estimate step-level advantages. However, training a critic adds computational overhead and struggles to accurately evaluate long interaction histories from sparse rewards ( Kazemnejad et al., 2025 ) . While recent work explores alternative step-level credit mechanisms, such as process reward models ( Lightman et al., 2024 ) , Monte-Carlo continuations ( Kazemnejad et al., 2025 ) , or outcome-conditioned heuristics ( Tan et al., 2026 ) , they often require human annotations, extra rollout budgets, or rely on proxy metrics. To overcome these limitations, we introduce LLM Value Function RL (LVRL), a method that extracts dense, per-step credit using a strong, frozen LLM as a value critic. By evaluating completed trajectories in hindsight, the frozen LLM critic observes downstream consequences to accurately assess earlier actions, such as ignored tool errors or successful recoveries. Because value estimation depends on the acting policy, we make the frozen LLM policy-aware through in-context learning. Specifically, we condition the estimator on summaries of other rollouts from the same task, along with their empirical success rate and final rewards. This dynamically updates the critic’s context with the current policy’s behavior and task performance, without requiring any parameter updates. We then convert the predicted values into step-level advantages via consecutive value differences ( Ng et al., 1999 ) . Crucially, by anchoring the initial state to the group success rate and the terminal state to the observed final reward, we guarantee that these step-level advantages sum exactly to the trajectory’s overall group-relative return. The frozen critic thus redistributes sparse outcome rewards across individual actions. We further extend this credit assignment technique to on-policy distillation (OPD), where a stronger teacher provides token-level supervision ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Gu et al., 2024 ) . Since uniform distillation penalizes large KL divergence everywhere, it can suppress alternative yet successful strategies discovered by the student. To align distillation with the capabilities of the student, LVOPD introduces value-guided gating . By restricting teacher supervision to actions that decrease the estimated value, we selectively correct execution errors while preserving the student’s independent progress. We train and evaluate LVRL and LVOPD on AppWorld, BabyAI, and SWE-bench Verified across policy scales ranging from 4B to 32B parameters. In LVRL, we utilize Claude Opus 4.6 as the frozen LLM value critic. LVRL consistently improves final generalization over outcome-only supervision (GRPO) and learned value functions (PPO). For instance, on Qwen3-8B, LVRL achieves 26.3 % 26.3\% success on AppWorld and 20.2 % 20.2\% on SWE-bench Verified, compared to 19.8 % 19.8\% and 12.0 % 12.0\% for GRPO, respectively. Notably, LVRL is particularly critical in environments requiring extended exploration: on BabyAI, it reaches 65.5 % 65.5\% success on out-of-distribution scenarios, whereas baseline methods fail entirely. Furthermore, LVOPD yields consistent improvements over standard distillation baselines on AppWorld, reaching a 20.2 % 20.2\% success rate with Qwen3-4B and improving pure OPD by 3.2 3.2 percentage points. Figure 1 : Overview of the proposed framework. ( 1 ) Group rollout: We sample a group of trajectories from the current policy and use their sparse outcome rewards to compute the empirical group success rate μ G \mu_{G} . ( 2 ) LLM value estimation: A frozen LLM critic scores all trajectory states, conditioned on group context. Estimates are anchored to empirical outcomes: the initial-state value to the group success rate and the terminal-state value to the actual reward. ( 3 ) Step advantages: We compute unnormalized step advantages as consecutive value differences ( A ¯ t = V ϕ ​ ( s t + 1 ) − V ϕ ​ ( s t ) \overline{A}_{t}=V_{\phi}(s_{t+1})-V_{\phi}(s_{t}) ) and normalize them across the group, yielding a dense, per-action credit signal. ( 4 ) Policy optimization: These step-level advantages drive standard PPO updates in LVRL, or act as a gating mechanism in LVOPD to restrict teacher supervision to actions that decrease the estimated value. Finally, we analyze the accuracy of the frozen LLM critic’s value predictions. Using Monte-Carlo rollouts as a ground-truth probe, we demonstrate that predicted value changes correctly identify 72 72 % of critical pitfalls and 66 66 % of recoveries. Furthermore, our ablations highlight two insights: in-context policy calibration is important for maximizing improvements, and the method’s overall efficacy is bounded by the capability of the chosen LLM critic. In summary, we present a unified framework for leveraging a frozen, policy-aware LLM to provide per-action credit assignment to guide RL and on-policy distillation, all without critic updates. 2 Related Work Step-level credit assignment for LLM agents. Classical actor–critic methods address temporal credit assignment by learning a parameterized value function ( Schulman et al., 2015 ; Schulman et al., 2017 ) , an approach extended to multi-turn language agents by ArCHer ( Zhou et al., 2024 ) and GenAC ( Shan et al., 2026 ) . To avoid the overhead of critic optimization, recent methods explore alternative credit mechanisms. The GRPO family of algorithms ( Shao et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025 ; Yu et al., 2025 ) relies on group-relative trajectory returns, uniformly assigning the same advantage to all actions within a rollout. Another line of work relies on extensive Monte-Carlo sampling; VinePPO ( Kazemnejad et al., 2025 ) explicitly rolls out continuations from intermediate states to estimate state values, whereas GiGPO ( Feng et al., 2025 ) and SALT ( Li et al., 2026a ) achieve a similar effect implicitly by aggregating returns over shared states across multiple trajectories. Other approaches rely on auxiliary models or proxy signals. Process reward models are trained with intermediate supervision ( Lightman et al., 2024 ; Zhou et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025b ; Xi et al., 2026 ; Wu et al., 2026 ) , while implicit estimators derive step- or token-level credit from hindsight judgments of the policy LLM ( Tan et al., 2026 ) , target-answer likelihoods ( Wang et al., 2025a ; Tao et al., 2026 ; Oh et al., 2026 ) , or internal signals of the policy, such as the discounted KL divergence of subsequent tokens ( Ma et al., 2026 ) , policy-to-reference log-ratios ( Kang et al., 2026 ) , and attention patterns ( Li et al., 2025 ) . Since these implicit estimators are tailored for single-turn reasoning with static answers, adapting them to multi-turn agentic tasks would require non-trivial modifications to handle dynamic environment feedback, complicating direct comparisons. Conceptually related to our approach, GVL ( Ma et al., 2025 ) uses a frozen vision-language model to estimate task progress from robot videos via in-context learning. However, GVL produces policy-agnostic progress scores. LVRL conditions the LLM on rollouts from the current policy and explicitly anchors its predictions to observed outcomes. This formulation ensures that the estimated values are both dynamically policy-aware and consistent with actual environment returns. On-policy distillation. Knowledge distillation transfers capabilities from a stronger teacher to a student model ( Hinton et al., 2015 ) . For generative tasks, on-policy distillation (OPD) mitigates exposure bias by evaluating the teacher on prefixes generated by the student ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ) , often optimizing a reverse-KL objective ( Gu et al., 2024 ) . However, standard token-level distillation is overly rigid, penalizing deviation from the teacher even when the student discovers a valid alternative strategy. Recent methods adapt teacher-guided updates using token- or step-level likelihood differences ( Jia et al., 2026 ; Zhong et al., 2026 ) , verifier rewards combined with teacher signals ( Akhondzadeh et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026 ; Lin et al., 2026 ) , or environment-informed teacher signals ( Zhou et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026b ) .
